children: By Lawrence G. McMillan
The put-call ratio is sending a strong message about Nvidia's stock, and history suggests a post-Thanksgiving 'bull spread' strategy for the Russell 2000 ETF
A computer program says the put-call ratio on Nvidia's stock is sending a buy signal.

We are entering what is normally a seasonally positive time of year, extending from the close of trading on the day before Thanksgiving through the second trading day of the next year. I will caution, though, that this seasonality had its worst year in December 2018, when the stock market was in a serious bearish decline.
As some have likened the current situation to 2018, a repeat might be the case this year. But the current decline has already had a substantial move prior to the projected seasonality.
There used to be three separate periods that were traded:
1) the post-Thanksgiving bullish period (usually the first two weeks after Thanksgiving)
2) the January effect, which originally occurred in January, but slipped back into December a few years ago
3) the Santa Claus rally, which encompasses the last five trading days of one year and the first two of the next year.

The first and third periods are bullish ones for the market as a whole. Period 2, however - the January effect - is a time when small-cap stocks outperform large-caps. Specifically, the Russell 2000 index of small-cap stocks RUT, tracked by the iShares Russell 2000 ETF IWM, outperforms the S&P 500 index SPX, which is tracked by the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF SPY.

The accompanying table shows the summation history for these three periods combined, going back to 1993, which is when the IWM ETF was first created. In each case, the data measure the gain or loss in SPX and RUT, beginning with the close of trading on the day before Thanksgiving and extending through the close of trading on the second day of the next year.

S&P 500 points  SPX % move  Russell 2000 points  RUT % move 
Total                   720.1         54.4%            354.2           81.8% 
Averages                 21.2          1.6%            10.4             2.4 
Wins                      26                            25 
Losses                    8                              9 
Avg. win                 51.2           3%             37.8             4.8% 
Avg. loss               -76.5          -3%             -65.5           -4.3% 
Max win                  145           10%             151.7           10.8% 
Max loss                 -202         -7.6%           -157.7           -10.6% 
                                                               McMillan Analysis

The S&P 500 has advanced 26 times in the 34 years covered by this data, while the Russell 2000 has advanced 25 times. The average advance for the S&P 500 (including losing years as well as winning years) has been 1.6%, but the Russell 2000 has advanced a much stronger 2.4% on average.

For that reason, we prefer to use IWM options in this trade. We use options because we know that our risk is limited to the prices we pay for the IWM calls. If we were to buy IWM or SPY ETFs, or futures on the indexes, our risk would be unknown should the market plunge during the time period.

A few times, the two indexes have diverged. Those periods were December 2004, December 2006 and December 2021. That means that SPX was up and RUT was down, or vice versa - that the two indexes diverged in their performance that year. That has happened only three times, with the last one from December 2021 to Jan. 4, 2022. That year was the end of a strong bull market, and SPX was flying higher, while RUT was already turning down in anticipation of the bear market that unfolded in 2022.

It is meaningful to know just how often RUT outperforms SPX. It turns out that SPX has had the best performance in 13 years, while RUT has been the better performer in 21 years. That's significant enough that we want to own IWM and not SPY, as noted previously.

The best-performing year in terms of points gained was December 2023, as RUT gained 151.7 points, or 8.5%. The best percentage gain was 2012, when RUT gained 10.8%. As noted above, 2018 was the worst December. RUT lost 157.4 points, or 10.6% (SPX dropped 202 points, or 7.6%). Technically, the worst point performance was December 2023, when RUT lost 157.7 points (6.5%).

Since the losses can be large percentage-wise, we use options in this trade. That is, we buy IWM call options, giving us the right, but not the obligation, to buy the ETF at a predetermined price. In that way, we know what our maximum loss in terms of points can be.
Given the market's recent performance, one might rightfully be a little cautious about using the trade this year, but its track record is strong enough that it is recommended:
At the close of trading on Wednesday, Nov. 25 (the day before Thanksgiving) we recommend these two trades:
Buy 2 IWM (Jan. 15) at-the-money calls.
Sell 2 IWM (Jan. 15) calls with a strike price 25 points higher.

That "bull spread" options strategy should cost somewhere near 9 points ($900). In some years, we have just bought IWM calls outright. However, when options are expensive, it makes sense to use a call bull spread, which we are doing in this case.

Follow-up instructions: roll the entire spread up if IWM trades at the higher strike. Otherwise, we plan to hold the spread until the second trading day of the new year, Tuesday, Jan. 5, 2027. Thus, the entire premium paid for the spread is at risk if IWM has declined from now until then.
Nvidia option traders got very pessimistic. So is it time to buy?
The damage to Nvidia's stock (NVDA) has been huge recently. The weighted put-call ratio chart is shown below.
One can see that the put-call ratio exploded as the stock was falling. That reflected extremely heavy pessimism on the part of option buyers. That is, they were loading up on put options.

Eventually, the put-call ratio will roll over and begin to trend downward. That will be a contrarian buy signal - that is, the put buyers are exhausted and it is time to be optimistic, not pessimistic.
There was a more modest selloff and concomitant put-call ratio peak last April (marked with a red "B" on the chart). That buy signal preceded a strong rally.
Now, after this week's sharp reversal on the news that the company has re-hired its former CEO, the stock bolted upward. But what has the put-call ratio done? It has rolled over by a tiny amount.

We use a computer program to analyze these charts, and that program is calling this a buy signal. In other words, the computer analysis thinks that a peak is forming on the put-call ratio chart. That conclusion is partially because the computer logic has some "mean reversion" built in. That is, with the put-call ratio so high historically, there is a good chance it will roll over and decline (i.e., revert to the mean).

Personally, I would prefer to see the put-call ratio continue to decline for another day or two before stepping in, so that the ratio's buy signal looks more like the one last April, where the actual buy, as denoted by the vertical line, came a couple of days after the ratio peaked. I think there is a good chance that could happen again this time.
